finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes the unvalidated `target` query parameter to http.Get and streams the response body back. An attacker can make the server request internal services, loopback or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/) and read the full response.
finding.sink: http.Get(target) (main.go:16), with the body returned via io.Copy(w, resp.Body) (main.go:22)

trace.note: /fetch is registered to the fetch handler with no authentication
target is read from the query string
http.Get is called on the raw value with no scheme, host or IP check
the response body is copied to the attacker (full-read SSRF); error text is also echoed at line 18

finding.guards_checked: None on this path: no allowlist, no scheme check, no private-IP or DNS pinning check, no custom dialer. The `allowed` map is used only by safeFetch. /safe (safeFetch, main.go:25-38) was also checked and not reported. It requires u.Hostname() to be in a fixed allowlist, and http.Get is called on u.String() of the same parsed URL, so there is no parse differential. I did not find a bypass without an open redirect on an allowlisted host. http.Get follows redirects by default, so that residual risk exists but cannot be confirmed from this code.

verdict.reason: main.go:15-16 passes the raw `target` query parameter to http.Get with no validation, /fetch is registered without auth at main.go:41, and the body is returned at main.go:22. The `allowed` check at main.go:27 applies only to /safe.
